# Introduction {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

<!----
TODO: Explain why there are three clusters (not 1) and how they differ.

## Where we're heading

In this and the next few weeks, you will learn to run
command-line bioinformatics programs at OSC step by step:

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

1. Additional details about OSC _(this lecture)_
2. How to use software at OSC, including programs that aren't installed _(next lecture)_
3. How to write shell scripts _(next week)_
4. How to submit shell scripts as "batch jobs" _(in two weeks)_
5. How to build functional commands to run such programs _(throughout)_

## Learning goals

This session follows up on the
[initial OSC introduction in week 2](../week02/w2b_osc.qmd),
and goes a bit deeper into:

- OSC Projects
- Cores
- OSC file systems
- Compute node types and access

# OSC Projects {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## OSC Projects

In this course, we exclusively use the course's OSC Project `PAS3493`.
For your own research, you would likely use a Project specific to a research
project or grant, or your lab's general-use Project.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Using a Project]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- Storing data in its dirs in `/fs/ess` and/or `/fs/scratch`
- Selecting the Project when starting compute jobs,
  like Code Server and (later in the course) batch jobs

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}

### [Managing a Project]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Generally only done by PIs
([more info](https://www.osc.edu/supercomputing/support/account){target="_blank"}).
Project administrators can, among others:

- Manage the compute budget and `/fs/ess` storage allocation
- Add users to the Project

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
If a new user doesn't have an OSC account yet, they will get an invite email ---
you can't create an account unless you've been added to a Project.
:::

:::
:::

::: footer
:::

## OSC billing

OSC bills **Projects** (not individual users), and only for two things:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%" .box-blue .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
### File storage

Storage in the Project dirs (`/fs/ess`), per TB per month.

:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%" .box-amber .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
### Compute

Compute node usage per "**core hour**":\
using 2 cores for 2 hours = 4 core hours.

:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%" .box-teal .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
### Who pays?

- Every OSU PI gets a $1,000 credit.
- OSU colleges pay some or all of the costs --- CFAES currently pays all of it.

:::
:::

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Prices for academic usage are generally low, but a Project using dozens of TBs
and hundreds of thousands of core hours could be charged several thousand dollars per year.
:::

# Cores {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Cores

In week 2, you learned that a supercomputer center has multiple supercomputers,
each of which consists of many nodes. But there is one more "level":

![](../img/terminology.png){fig-align="center" width="95%" fig-alt="A diagram showing how the terms core/processor, node, and cluster/supercomputer fit together." .lightbox}

. . .

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [What is a core?]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

A component of a computer (node) that can (semi-)independently
perform a computing task, like running a bioinformatics program.

Many programs can use **multiple cores** for a single run,
which can speed things up considerably.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Core / Processor / CPU / Thread]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

These terms are not technically synonyms,
but are often used interchangeably.

For working at OSC, treat them as meaning the same thing:
the components of a node that can be reserved and used independently.

:::
:::

::: footer
:::

## Quiz: Core hours

::: callout-quiz
::: callout-note
#### Think about it

A) You run a program with 8 reserved cores for 3 hours.
   How many core hours will your OSC Project be billed for?

B) Afterwards, you find out that the program only ever used 1 of those cores.
   Does that change the number of billed core hours?
   What does this tell you about how many cores to request?

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

<!-----
<details><summary> {{< fa square-check >}} &nbsp; &nbsp; _Click for the answers_</summary>

A) 8 cores × 3 hours = **24 core hours**.

B) **No**: you're billed for the cores you _reserved_, whether or not they were used.
   So request multiple cores only if the program can actually use them
   (check its documentation!) --- otherwise you waste resources
   and, as you'll see later, may also wait longer for your job to start.

</details>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
------>
:::
:::

# File systems {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## OSC file systems

An expanded version of the table from week 2:

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

| File system   | Located within        | Quota                 | Backed up?    | Auto-purged?          | One for each... |
|---------------|-----------------------|-----------------------|---------------|-----------------------|-----------------|
| **Home**      | `/users/`             | 500 GB / 1 M files    | Yes           | No                    | User            |
| **Project**   | `/fs/ess/`            | Flexible              | Yes           | No                    | OSC Project     |
| **Scratch**   | `/fs/scratch/`        | 100 TB                | No            | After 60 days         | OSC Project     |
| **Compute**   | `$TMPDIR`             | 1 TB                  | No            | After job completes   | Compute job     |

: {.striped .hover}

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: callout-tip
#### Recommendation
For your own research,
**work mostly in the Project dir** (`/fs/ess/`),
which offers backed-up, permanent storage with flexible quota.
:::

## When are the other file systems useful?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%" .box-blue .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
### Home

**Drawbacks**: limited space that can't be expanded,
and harder to share files with collaborators.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

**Useful for**: files you use across projects, like some software.
Also stores user-specific settings, in hidden files (`.`) that you should
generally leave alone.

:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%" .box-amber .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
### Scratch

**Drawbacks**: temporary and not backed up.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

**Useful for**: large datasets, thanks to _effectively unlimited_ space and
_faster_ read/write ("I/O") speed.
Run analyses here, then copy key files to the Project dir.

:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%" .box-teal .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
### Compute

**Drawbacks**: extremely fleeting --- files are deleted as soon as the job stops.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

**Useful for**: very I/O-intensive jobs, with even faster I/O.
But it requires extra code in your script, so I rarely use it.

:::
:::

## Home dir clarifications & other notes

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}

### [Home dir clarifications]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- The project number in your Home dir path (e.g., `/users/PAS3454/jane`)
  is merely a naming convention:
  your Home dir is not really tied to any OSC Project.
  It stays the same if you're removed from a Project or the Project stops existing.

- You land in your Home dir after logging in,
  but this is typically not where you want to be to work with data.

- Avoid storing research project files in your Home dir.

- Home dir will have hidden files (those starting with a `.`) that are generated
  and used automatically by software.
  Don't mess with them unless you know what you're doing!

:::
::: {.column width="5%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="43%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

::: {.callout-note}
#### Accessing back-ups
Home and Project dirs are backed up daily.
You don't have _direct_ access to the backups,
but you can email OSC to restore your files to the way they were on a specific date.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
#### Files on different clusters
File systems are shared among OSC's clusters,
so you can access your files in the exact same way
regardless of which cluster you're connected to.
:::

:::
:::

::: footer
:::

## Quiz: Which file system?

::: callout-quiz
::: callout-note
#### What would happen, or what would you do?

A) Three days ago, you accidentally deleted a script from your dir in `/fs/scratch`.
   Can OSC restore it?

B) You ran an analysis in `/fs/scratch` in March and didn't look at the results
   until June. What might you find?

C) A program creates millions of small temporary files while running.
   Why would it be a bad idea to have it write these to your Home dir?

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

<!-----
<details><summary> {{< fa square-check >}} &nbsp; &nbsp; _Click for the answers_</summary>

A) **No**: Scratch is not backed up. Only Home and Project dirs are.

B) The results **may be gone**: files in Scratch are automatically purged after 60 days.
   Copy results you want to keep to the Project dir.

C) Home dirs have a quota of **1 million files** (not just 500 GB),
   and Home also has slower I/O than Scratch ---
   a Scratch dir would be a better choice.

</details>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
------>
:::
:::

# Compute nodes {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Compute node types

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### ["Standard" nodes]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- By far the most numerous (e.g., Pitzer has 564)
- Even these vary in size, e.g. from 40-48 cores per node on Pitzer
- Used by default, and will serve you well for most omics analyses

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Other node types]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- Nodes with extra memory: `largemem` and `hugemem`
- Nodes with GPUs (Graphical Processing Units) rather than CPUs

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
You may occasionally need these, for example for genome or transcriptome assembly
(large-memory nodes) or Oxford Nanopore base-calling (GPU nodes).
:::

:::
:::

## Memory versus storage

When we talk about a computer's "memory", this refers to **RAM** ---
don't confuse this with file **storage**.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Memory (RAM)]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- The data a computer has actively "loaded" or in use
- Accessed _orders of magnitude_ faster than data on disk
- E.g., heavily used when you play a game or have many browser tabs open

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}

### [Storage (disk)]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- The data that is saved in files on disk
- When your computer freezes, it's typically because memory is full
  and disk storage has to be used as well

:::
:::

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Bioinformatics programs may load input data into memory for fast access,
and hold intermediate results there too.
With large datasets, they may need 10s or 100s of GBs of memory.
:::

## Using compute nodes

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [Compute jobs]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

You use compute nodes by **requesting resources**,
such as a number of nodes and cores, and for how long you need them.

These requests result in "**compute jobs**" (or simply "jobs").
Our VS Code sessions are an example!

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [The job scheduler]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Many users send requests all the time,
so a **job scheduler** (**Slurm** at OSC) considers each request
and assigns resources to jobs as they become available.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
In two weeks, you'll learn to submit scripts as "batch jobs" with Slurm.
:::

:::
:::

## Quiz: True or false?

::: callout-quiz
::: callout-note
#### True or false?

A) If a program crashes because it runs out of memory,
   moving your files to a location with a larger storage quota will fix it.

B) Requesting 8 cores instead of 1 will make any program run about 8× faster.

C) A file you created while connected to Pitzer can also be accessed from Cardinal.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

<!-----
<details><summary> {{< fa square-check >}} &nbsp; &nbsp; _Click for the answers_</summary>

A) **False**: memory (RAM) is not storage.
   You would need to request more memory, possibly on a `largemem` node.

B) **False**: the program has to support using multiple cores,
   and even then, the speed-up is usually less than proportional.

C) **True**: file systems are shared among OSC's clusters.

</details>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
------>
:::
:::

The **Clusters** dropdown menu also gives direct access to a Unix shell on Ascend,
Cardinal, or Pitzer. For example, via `Cardinal Shell Access`:

![](../img/ondemand_shell-cardinal.png){fig-align="center" width="68%" fig-alt="A screenshot of a Unix shell opened via the Clusters menu on OSC OnDemand." .lightbox}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
In this course, you access a shell via Code Server instead,
but this method can occasionally be useful as a quicker access point.
:::

## Citing and contacting OSC

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [Citing OSC]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

When you use OSC, it's good practice to **acknowledge and cite OSC** in your papers ---
see their [citation page](https://www.osc.edu/resources/getting_started/citation){target="_blank"}.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Contacting OSC]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Email **<oschelp@osc.edu>** with questions like:

- Problems with your account
- Installing or using specific software
- Why your jobs keep failing

They are usually very quick to respond!

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
If you don't have an account yet, use <start@osc.edu> instead.
:::
